main.title: How your phone knows where you are
main.paragraph: GPS is a {constellation} of more than 30 satellites about 20,200 kilometres up, each carrying {atomic clocks}.[1] Every satellite keeps broadcasting its exact time and its exact position. Your phone hears four or more of them and, from each signal's {travel time}, works out its distance to each satellite; {trilateration} then turns those distances into a position.[2] The phone's own clock is cheap and slightly off, so every distance carries the same unknown error, which is why each one is called a {pseudorange}. A fourth satellite supplies the extra equation that solves for that clock error, so GPS needs four satellites, not three.[3] One more correction keeps it honest: by {relativity}, clocks on the satellites gain about 38 microseconds a day on clocks on the ground, which would add roughly 10 kilometres of error every day, so they are set to tick slower before launch.[4]

terms.definition: A set of satellites spread around the Earth so that enough of them are always overhead. GPS keeps at least 24 in six orbits, circling the Earth every 12 hours.
Clocks that count the vibrations of atoms, which never vary. They drift by far less than a microsecond a day, which is what makes a satellite's time stamp trustworthy.
A distance worked out with a clock that may be off. All of a phone's pseudoranges share the same clock error, so the error can be solved for along with the position.

Einstein's finding that time runs at different rates for different observers. Satellite clocks run faster because gravity is weaker up there, and slightly slower because they move fast; the net gain is about 38 microseconds a day.

figure.label: Four satellites broadcast their time and position; the signals reach your phone, which solves for its position, height and its own clock error; the satellite clocks are corrected for relativity.

parts.caption: Clocks set slow to cancel relativity

explainer.name: Relativity correction
explainer.what: Without it the satellite clocks would run 38 microseconds a day fast, and positions would drift by about 10 km a day. The clocks are tuned slow before launch to cancel it.

explainer.name: Your phone
explainer.what: Measures each signal's travel time, turns it into a pseudorange, and solves four equations for its position and its own clock error.

explainer.what: Latitude, longitude, height, and the phone's clock error. A phone is usually accurate to within a few metres in the open.

levels.question: Do you fully understand how a signal's travel time tells you a distance?
levels.title: Distance from travel time
levels.paragraph: You can measure a distance without a ruler if you know how fast something moves and how long it took to arrive. In a storm, count the seconds between the flash and the {thunder}: sound covers about a kilometre every three seconds, so the count tells you how far away the lightning struck.[1] The same works for a {radio signal}, which moves at the {speed of light}, almost 300,000 kilometres per second.[2] Distance is speed multiplied by {travel time}. Radio is so fast that a single {microsecond}, one millionth of a second, already stands for 300 metres. That makes the clocks critical: if the sender's and the receiver's clocks disagree by one microsecond, the distance comes out 300 metres wrong.[3]

terms.definition: The sound of a lightning strike. Light from the flash reaches you almost at once, while the sound travels at about 343 metres per second, so the delay between them grows with distance.
A message carried by radio waves, a kind of light our eyes cannot see. Phones, radios and satellites all talk this way.
The speed at which light and radio waves travel through empty space: exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. Nothing carries a signal faster.
How long a signal takes from the moment it is sent to the moment it arrives: the arrival time minus the send time, read from two clocks.
One millionth of a second. At the speed of light a signal covers about 300 metres in that time.

figure.label: A sender's clock and a receiver's clock; a radio signal crosses between them; the travel time times the speed of light gives 300 metres; a clock error of one microsecond doubles it.

explainer.what: The receiver notes when the signal arrives. The difference from the send time is the travel time: here one microsecond.

explainer.name: Distance
explainer.what: Speed of light multiplied by the travel time. One microsecond of travel is 300 metres.

explainer.what: If the receiver's clock runs one microsecond late, the travel time looks twice as long and the distance doubles. Every microsecond of error adds 300 metres.

levels.question: Do you fully understand how a few distances pin down one exact point?
levels.title: Finding a point from distances
levels.paragraph: If you know how far you are from one landmark, you could be anywhere on a circle around it at that distance. A second known distance draws a second circle, and the two circles cross at just two points. A third distance, from a third landmark, settles it: only one point lies on all three circles. This method is called {trilateration}.[1] It needs no angles and no compass, only the distances and the exact positions of the {reference points}. Out in three dimensions each distance draws a {sphere} instead of a circle. Three spheres meet at two points, and one of them is usually far off in space, so it can be ruled out; the {intersection} that remains gives height as well as place.[2]

terms.definition: Finding a position from distances to known points, by intersecting circles (or spheres) of those radii. It differs from triangulation, which uses angles.
Points whose exact positions are known in advance, like landmarks on a map. Each distance is measured from one of them.
The 3D version of a circle: every point at the same distance from a centre, in all directions. A distance measured in space puts you somewhere on a sphere.
The place where two or more shapes cross. The intersection of all the circles is the only position that matches every distance at once.

figure.label: Three circles around three reference points; each circle is the set of points at one measured distance; they cross at one point, which is your position.

parts.caption: One distance: you are on this circle

explainer.name: First distance
explainer.what: Every point on this circle is exactly that far from landmark 1. You are somewhere on it, but it could be anywhere.

connects.text: a second circle narrows it down

motion.description: The first circle draws itself around landmark 1.

parts.caption: A second distance leaves two points

explainer.name: Second distance
explainer.what: The circle around landmark 2 crosses the first at exactly two points. You are at one of them.

motion.description: The second circle draws itself and its two crossings light up.

parts.caption: A third distance picks the one point

explainer.name: Third distance
explainer.what: The circle around landmark 3 passes through only one of the two crossings, so that crossing is your position.

connects.text: rules out one of its two points

motion.description: The third circle draws itself through just one crossing.

parts.caption: The only point on all three

explainer.name: Your position
explainer.what: The single point that lies on every circle: the one place that is the right distance from all three landmarks.
